whyThisMatters: Real payroll and recruitment decisions are fast — a form arrives, a deadline looms, and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a familiar agent name, an urgent deadline, a portal migration notice. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why recognising an agent's name isn't the same as checking their domain.
Ask why checking despite a tight candidate deadline is included as a trick bubble here — it's not wrong, it's just the one people most often skip.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds familiar — a recognisable agent name, an urgent recruitment deadline, a portal-migration notice — without checking the exact domain or process behind it. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Used Crew Portal For Bank Updates
Called Back On Known HR Number
Replied With Bank Details By Email

bubbles.note: Recognising an agent's name is a reasonable first signal, but it isn't proof by itself — the exact sending domain is what actually confirms who sent it, since a familiar name can still come from a spoofed address.
Checking despite time pressure is exactly the right habit — it's included here as a trick because it's the one people most often skip under a tight deadline, not because it's wrong.

bubbles.text: Called The Number In The Text
bubbles.note: A number given inside a suspicious text may connect you straight to the attacker — only a number you already had counts as a real check.
A migration notice that asks for your password and bank details together through a link is exactly the pattern to distrust, however official it sounds.
